The learners I worry about least are the ones who come to me and say they have stopped improving. That sentence tells me they are paying attention. The plateau is visible to them, which means we can work on it. The ones I worry about are the ones who have not noticed. Here is what I see, again and again, with advanced learners. They understand almost everything. Their reading is excellent. But under pressure, in a meeting or on a call, they fall back on the three or four structures they trust, and the other twenty never leave the page. So I ask them for one thing, and only one. In every conversation, use one structure you are not completely sure of. Just one. It will cost you a few mistakes. That is the price of leaving your comfort zone, and in my experience it is the only price that has ever bought anybody any progress.

I am not a native speaker, and I have worked in English for most of my career, so I have had to find a way to measure it. What I do is simple. Once a month I record five minutes of myself talking about my week. Always the same topic, always without notes, always five minutes. Then I wait. You should never listen to the new recording on the same day, because on the same day you hear what you meant to say. A week later you hear what you actually said, and that is a very different thing. When I started, the first change was fluency. Fewer pauses, fewer restarts, less time looking for the beginning of a sentence. Accuracy followed about six months later, and it followed almost by itself, because once you stop fighting for every sentence, you have the attention left over to get it right.
